title: unstable map iteration order causes test to sometimes leave non-GA features disabled
body:
### What happened?

PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115324 was reverted by #116062 because it (erroneously) relied on OpenAPIV3 feature to be enabled, but `TestPodSecurityGAOnly` would non-deterministically leave the feature disabled after running.

I tracked it down to the fact that this test disables all `PreRelease` or `Beta` features in a loop which iterates over a `map`, which are known to have unstable iteration order:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e55f2a9b54e0f6bd9ed12e50752d7d2545ab0cab/test/integration/auth/podsecurity_test.go#L74-L81

When key `AllBeta` is processed before key `OpenAPIV3`, then `AllBeta` would disable `OpenAPIV3` before `OpenAPIV3`s default value is to be saved.

Normally, `AllBeta` ignores features that have been explicitly set, so it only affects those which fall back on the `Default` value. But this issue does not just affect `OpenAPIV3` but any non-GA feature.

I suggest the loop in `TestPodSecurityGAOnly` be made to skip the special feature keys such as `AllBeta`.

/cc @liggitt 
/cc @apel

### What did you expect to happen?

The value before every feature gate should be restored after running `TestPodSecurityGAOnly`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This test always fails on my machine (just pasted it into `test/integration/auth/podsecurity_test.go`):

```go
func TestRestoreFeatures(t *testing.T) {
	var targetFeature featuregate.Feature

	// Grab a beta feature form the list to test with
	for k, v := range utilfeature.DefaultMutableFeatureGate.GetAll() {
		if v.PreRelease == featuregate.Beta && v.Default {
			targetFeature = k
			break
		}
	}

	if len(targetFeature) == 0 {
		t.Log("no beta features to test against")
		return
	}

        // see if we iterate the feature map with AllBeta first within a few tries
	for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
		attemptFunc := func() bool {
			fg := utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.DeepCopy()
			originalValue := fg.Enabled(targetFeature)

			func() {
				// Disable all alpha and beta features
				for k, v := range fg.DeepCopy().GetAll() {
					if v.PreRelease == featuregate.Alpha || v.PreRelease == featuregate.Beta {
						defer featuregatetesting.SetFeatureGateDuringTest(t, fg, k, false)()
					}
				}
			}()

			return originalValue != fg.Enabled(targetFeature)
		}

		if attemptFunc() {
			t.Fatal("original value for feature not same as new value after restoration")
			break
		}
	}
}
```

title: Enabling APIServer tracing breaks port forwarding
body:
### What happened?

See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113791 for details.  When we graduated APIServer tracing to beta prior to the 1.26 release, it broke port-forwarding.

To fix this, the opentelemetry-go community agreed to cut a patch release for me: https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-contrib/issues/3513.

We need to update to otelhttp v0.35.1 to fix this.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable the APIServerTracing feature-gate, and run the [sig-instrumentation] MetricsGrabber tests.  Those fail consistently.

nodes.body:

/priority important-soon

/assign
/triage accepted
cc @kubernetes/sig-instrumentation-leads

title: Pod is running, but cannot allocate devices when the pod start before device plugin register right to kubelet
body:
### What happened?

A pod using gpu in our k8s cluster, when we delete kubelet_internal_checkpoint and restart the node where the pod is located. After the node start normally, we find that, the pod is running, but the gpu device is not mounted on the container of pod. If we delete container of the pod, the gpu device mount normally.
I think the reason is that the pod is start befor gpu device register right to kubelet.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod should not be running when device plugin not register to kubelet.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. a pod uses device such as gpu;
2. delete kubelet_internal_checkpoint;
3. reboot node;
4. check the device is mounted normally or not;

### Anything else we need to know?

 In the function  allocateContainerResources,  if isDevicePluginResource return false, kubelet will skip device allocation, however, if the device plugin not register right to kubelet and the kubelet_internal_checkpoint is lost, the function isDevicePluginResource will reture false, and generate the problem report.
      `func (m *ManagerImpl) allocateContainerResources(pod *v1.Pod, container *v1.Container, devicesToReuse map[string]sets.String) error {
	podUID := string(pod.UID)
	contName := container.Name
	allocatedDevicesUpdated := false
	// Extended resources are not allowed to be overcommitted.
	// Since device plugin advertises extended resources,
	// therefore Requests must be equal to Limits and iterating
	// over the Limits should be sufficient.
	for k, v := range container.Resources.Limits {
		resource := string(k)
		needed := int(v.Value())
		klog.V(3).Infof("needs %d %s", needed, resource)
		if !m.isDevicePluginResource(resource) {
			continue
		}
		// Updates allocatedDevices to garbage collect any stranded resources
		// before doing the device plugin allocation.
		if !allocatedDevicesUpdated {
			m.UpdateAllocatedDevices()
			allocatedDevicesUpdated = true
		}
		allocDevices, err := m.devicesToAllocate(podUID, contName, resource, needed, devicesToReuse[resource])`

```
      affinity:
```

Yes, `matchFields` is only designed for single nodeName matching term, specially, for daemonSet pod scheduling, you can use `matchExpressions` for multi matched values. But this is open, if you have other usercases than daemonSet, we can actually extend this field. @13567436138

title: e2e loadbalancer udp conntrack test not working properly on AWS variant
body:
### What happened?

When running the e2e tests on AWS, the following two tests are failing:

```
[sig-network] LoadBalancers should be able to preserve UDP traffic when server pod cycles for a LoadBalancer service on different nodes [Suite:openshift/conformance/parallel] [Suite:k8s]
```
```
[sig-network] LoadBalancers should be able to preserve UDP traffic when server pod cycles for a LoadBalancer service on the same nodes [Suite:openshift/conformance/parallel] [Suite:k8s]
```
with the stated cause being:
```
Error syncing load balancer: failed to ensure load balancer: Protocol UDP not supported by LoadBalancer
```

these tests were added with https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/113650


### What did you expect to happen?

Expected the tests to pass

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run the loadbalancer test suite on AWS

### Anything else we need to know?

While investigating the root cause of these failures, i cam across this function in the cloud-provider-aws:

https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-aws/blob/master/pkg/providers/v1/aws.go#L5226-L5236

```go
func checkProtocol(port v1.ServicePort, annotations map[string]string) error {
	// nlb supports tcp, udp
	if isNLB(annotations) && (port.Protocol == v1.ProtocolTCP || port.Protocol == v1.ProtocolUDP) {
		return nil
	}
	// elb only supports tcp
	if !isNLB(annotations) && port.Protocol == v1.ProtocolTCP {
		return nil
	}
	return fmt.Errorf("Protocol %s not supported by LoadBalancer", port.Protocol)
}
```

This function checks to ensure that a specific annotation has been applied to the Service object to determine if it is an NLB. The test in question creates the Service object with no annotations placed upon it, this in turn causes the test to fail.

This [discussion from slack with the AWS maintainers](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0LRMHZ1T/p1676481894305559) confirms the need for the user to add the annotation. It is a continuation of a discussion that started in the SIG Cloud Provider meeting from 15 Feb 2023.

### Kubernetes version

i don't have a live cluster for this anymore, but it was version 1.26.1

title: OIDC groups are not handles by default
body:
### What happened?

We are running Kubernetes with an OpenID connector. 
our API server is configured with 2 flags in this regard:

```console
      oidc-client-id: ourKubernetes
      oidc-issuer-url: https://our-openid-connect.tld
```

In our issuer, we have the `groups` key within the claims similar to: `{"sub": "john.doe", "groups": ["fake-users"]}`

When calling the API with the openID connect token, we see the user `john.doe` with no other group than `system:authenticated`

```console
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(command-to-retrieve-open-id-connect-token)" https://127.0.0.1:64835/apis/v1/services/kube-system -k
```

As seen in the access logs:

```console
docker exec kind-control-plane cat /var/log/kubernetes/kube-apiserver-audit.log | grep doe
```

```json
{
  "kind": "Event",
  "apiVersion": "audit.k8s.io/v1",
  "level": "Metadata",
  "auditID": "0c411999-4321-47e2-8d0f-54b3d347374b",
  "stage": "ResponseComplete",
  "requestURI": "/apis/v1/services/kube-system",
  "verb": "list",
  "user": {
    "username": "https://our-openid-connect.tld#john.doe",
    "groups": [
      "system:authenticated"
    ]
  },
  "sourceIPs": [
    "172.18.0.1"
  ],
  "userAgent": "curl/7.85.0",
  "objectRef": {
    "resource": "kube-system",
    "apiGroup": "v1",
    "apiVersion": "services"
  },
  "responseStatus": {
    "metadata": {},
    "status": "Failure",
    "reason": "Forbidden",
    "code": 403
  },
  "requestReceivedTimestamp": "2023-02-22T10:41:34.796559Z",
  "stageTimestamp": "2023-02-22T10:41:34.866302Z",
  "annotations": {
    "authorization.k8s.io/decision": "forbid",
    "authorization.k8s.io/reason": ""
  }
}
```


Adding the parameter `oidc-groups-claim: groups` and repeating the access with openID token, we can note that the groups are correctly taken from the openID token:

```json
{
  "kind": "Event",
  "apiVersion": "audit.k8s.io/v1",
  "level": "Metadata",
  "auditID": "9bd727b9-4fc3-4178-a915-29635abb2ace",
  "stage": "ResponseComplete",
  "requestURI": "/apis/v1/services/kube-system",
  "verb": "list",
  "user": {
    "username": "https://our-openid-connect.tld#john.doe",
    "groups": [
      "fake-users",
      "system:authenticated"
    ]
  },
  "sourceIPs": [
    "172.18.0.1"
  ],
  "userAgent": "curl/7.85.0",
  "objectRef": {
    "resource": "kube-system",
    "apiGroup": "v1",
    "apiVersion": "services"
  },
  "responseStatus": {
    "metadata": {},
    "status": "Failure",
    "reason": "Forbidden",
    "code": 403
  },
  "requestReceivedTimestamp": "2023-02-22T10:30:42.054262Z",
  "stageTimestamp": "2023-02-22T10:30:42.391581Z",
  "annotations": {
    "authorization.k8s.io/decision": "forbid",
    "authorization.k8s.io/reason": ""
  }
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

According to the [documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authentication/#configuring-the-api-server), the default value are `--oidc-username-claim=sub`, `--oidc-groups-claim=groups` and `--oidc-groups-prefix=oidc:`

With this, we should expect the user to be authenticated with groups `oidc:fake-users` in addition to `system:authenticated`


```json
{
  "kind": "Event",
  "apiVersion": "audit.k8s.io/v1",
  "level": "Metadata",
  "auditID": "9bd727b9-4fc3-4178-a915-29635abb2ace",
  "stage": "ResponseComplete",
  "requestURI": "/apis/v1/services/kube-system",
  "verb": "list",
  "user": {
    "username": "https://our-openid-connect.tld#john.doe",
    "groups": [
      "oidc:fake-users",
      "system:authenticated"
    ]
  },
  "sourceIPs": [
    "172.18.0.1"
  ],
  "userAgent": "curl/7.85.0",
  "objectRef": {
    "resource": "kube-system",
    "apiGroup": "v1",
    "apiVersion": "services"
  },
  "responseStatus": {
    "metadata": {},
    "status": "Failure",
    "reason": "Forbidden",
    "code": 403
  },
  "requestReceivedTimestamp": "2023-02-22T10:30:42.054262Z",
  "stageTimestamp": "2023-02-22T10:30:42.391581Z",
  "annotations": {
    "authorization.k8s.io/decision": "forbid",
    "authorization.k8s.io/reason": ""
  }
}
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a kind cluster with some openID connect configuration

```console
cat <<EOF > audit-policy.yaml
apiVersion: [audit.k8s.io/v1](http://audit.k8s.io/v1)

cat <<EOF > kind-config.yaml

nodes:
- role: control-plane
  kubeadmConfigPatches:
  - |
    kind: ClusterConfiguration
    apiServer:
      extraArgs:
        oidc-client-id: my-cluster
        oidc-issuer-url: https://our-openid-connect.tld
        audit-log-path: /var/log/kubernetes/kube-apiserver-audit.log
        audit-policy-file: /etc/kubernetes/policies/audit-policy.yaml
      extraVolumes:
        - name: audit-policies
          hostPath: /etc/kubernetes/policies
          mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/policies
          readOnly: true
          pathType: "DirectoryOrCreate"
        - name: "audit-logs"
          hostPath: "/var/log/kubernetes"
          mountPath: "/var/log/kubernetes"
          readOnly: false
          pathType: DirectoryOrCreate
  # mount the local file on the control plane
  extraMounts:
  - hostPath: ./audit-policy.yaml
    containerPath: /etc/kubernetes/policies/audit-policy.yaml
    readOnly: true
EOF

kind create cluster --image kindest/node:v1.23.1 --config kind-config.yaml
```

_No response_

title: GKE - Multi cluster services stopped work after DNS zone was removed
body:
### What happened?

[MCS](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/multi-cluster-services) mechanism to communicate multiple GKE clusters stopped work in all our clusters since 09.02.2023. We noticed that MCS service account (`service-PROJ_NUMBER@gcp-sa-mcsd.iam.gserviceaccount.com`)  deleted the private DNS zone in Cloud DNS `gke-multi-cluster-service-NUMBER` which was used by that mechanism to resolve cross cluster services domain names `SERVICE_EXPORT_NAME.NAMESPACE.svc.clusterset.local`

Currently communication between clusters works only through auto-generated service resources (`gke-mcs-ik7gi8ughg`)

### What did you expect to happen?

Should be possibility to resolve DNS names `SERVICE_EXPORT_NAME.NAMESPACE.svc.clusterset.local` in MCS mechanism

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create two GKE clusters in GCP: first and second
2. Enable MCS mechanism based on https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/multi-cluster-services
3. Create in second cluster example `Service` (namespace: `default`)
4. Export `Service` from second cluster by creating `ServiceExport` resource
5. Try to connect to the `Service` from first cluster by `example.default.svc.clusterset.local`

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

is similar

If ping latency is large, the DNS will be slow too. I am not sure about how to dig into this.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6450081/218442527-d4eadadb-1446-47b5-922d-a68ccfe936ec.png)

I wonder if was because of this https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114229
or https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114181

it seems that the network programming latency going down is related to the networklatency and dnslookup going up
/cc @dlapcevic @aojea

This is a huge regression for DNS lookup latency.

It seems strange that https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114229 or https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114181 would impact DNS lookup latency, since it greatly improved network programming latency.

The only thing that I can think of is that the CPU is the bottleneck now, since resyncing iptables is done so frequently.

The CPU increase in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114229#issuecomment-1346566684 https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6450081/207064716-1dc8cab8-1c63-4773-a7a5-37a3221eae30.png is showing a significant increase on 100 node test, but this is 5k, so it might be the issue here.
ok, then let me revert https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114229

### What happened?

When constructing a `rest.Request`, _e.g._ to stream I/O from a pod:

```
	req := k8s.CoreV1().RESTClient().Post().Resource("pods").Name(podName).Namespace(podNamespace).SubResource("exec")
	req.VersionedParams(&v1.PodExecOptions{
		Command: command,
		Stdin:   false,
		Stdout:  true,
		Stderr:  true,
		TTY:     true,
	}, scheme.ParameterCodec)
	exec, err := remotecommand.NewSPDYExecutor(config, "POST", req.URL())
```

if `req.err` ends up set, `req.URL()` will still return a result without indicating that something went wrong, resulting in a misleading error further down the line. (In my case, I wasn’t providing the correct scheme; the parameters therefore couldn’t be encoded, and the SPDY upgrade failed with an error saying that at least one of stdin, stdout or stderr had to be provided.)

### What did you expect to happen?

Other operations on `rest.Request` fails as appropriate if `req.err` is not `nil`; I would expect `URL()` to do so too. I realise that means a backwards-incompatible change.

Another solution could be to provide a `req.Error()` (same as on the response).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See above, with any scheme other than client-go’s.

nodes.title: Fix legacy fallback stale for aggregated discovery
nodes.body:
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Fixes legacy fallback returning no resources for API Services that share the same service object.

The test does exercise this specific case, but I don't know if it's the best we can do. The bug reproduces only in the scenario that the number of APIServices added exceeds the amount that the workers are able to process concurrently (current 2 workers https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/apiserver/handler_discovery.go#L402, so the test has three APIServices).

In this specific case, lastMarkedDirty is set to a time before the first request to the legacy fallback and subsequent calls to fetchFreshDiscoveryForService will use the cached version rather than fetching from the legacy endpoint.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/apiserver/handler_discovery.go#L182-L187

The cache is problematic because we cache the entire service as a whole. However in the case of the legacy fallback, only the resources for one group-version is fetched so we should not cache it as the return value for the entire service since it can also serve other group-versions.

@deads2k has an alternate fix that involves partitioning the cache by APIService rather than by service, it's about the same performance if every service has a legacy fallback, but is probably slightly inefficient once the service migrates to use aggregated discovery: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115728

title: MultiCIDRRangeAllocator requires node reboot to assign ranges
body:
### What happened?

When the `ClusterCIDR` is created *after* a node has booted, addresses are not defined;

```
> kubectl get cc -A
No resources found
> kubectl create -f kubernetes/clustercidr.yaml
clustercidr.networking.k8s.io/default created
> kubectl get cc -A
NAME      PERNODEHOSTBITS   IPV4          IPV6         AGE
default   8                 11.0.0.0/16   1100::/112   5s
> kubectl get node -o json vm-002 | jq .spec
{}
# (reboot node vm-002 ...)
> kubectl get node -o json vm-002 | jq .spec
{
  "podCIDR": "11.0.0.0/24",
  "podCIDRs": [
    "11.0.0.0/24",
    "1100::/120"
  ]
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Addresses shall be allocated for all nodes with empty `spec.podCIDRs` when a `ClusterCIDR` is created (*then* they become immutable).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Probably the easiest way is to check the controller:

* Create the controller with MultiCIDRRangeAllocator enabled and configured
* Create a `ClusterCIDR`
* Check the node.spec on the controller
* Reboot it
* Check again


### Anything else we need to know?

I can't see a clean way to start a cluster without this fixed. It the cni-plugin requires spec.podCIDRs to work the node will not become ready until it's rebooted.

As a work-around in my test env I can create a controller that is _not a node_ in the cluster (I think k3s and AWS does like this).

### Kubernetes version

v1.27.0-alpha.1.228+0e3818e02760af



### Cloud provider

### OS version

Linux

body:
### What happened?

```yaml


apiVersion: apps/v1

  name: alpine
  labels:
    app: alpine

  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: alpine

    spec:

        image: alpine
        volumeMounts:
        - name: cm
          mountPath: /var/run/cm
      volumes:
      - name: cm
        configMap:
          name: fake
```

Apply this deployment, immediately after `kubectl delete deployment alpine`.

The pod is scheduled and moves to Terminating. However, it doesn't actually get removed for a long time after. Seems about 1 min (termination period is 30s)

Pod removes ~instantly.

See above, just create a deployment that cannot mount and delete things.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

If the ipFamilyPolicy is RequireDualStack, then the ip list of each endpoint coming from hns will have 2 IPs (IPV4 and IPV6). title: client-go: set the default of the 'host' label to an empty string for client metrics
body:
### What happened?

the default value of the `host`  label is `none` for all client metrics, see

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1f02f43ec6910cbcd46222b16a2f3965458e5e45/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request.go#L792-L795

in a query, we want the user to use `{host!=""}` rather than `{host!="none"}`.
in reality, the `RESTClient.base` may never be empty, so the label is never set to `none` in a real cluster?

nodes.body: /cc @dgrisonnet
/sig api-machinery
how can you get a metrics with host=none? that request will never work

I guess the intent is more to have the empty string as a sane default rather "none" as it is more intuitive to the users when querying (if there is even a scenario when that is necessary). This is more of a cleanup than anything really.

> how can you get a metrics with host=none? that request will never work

I don't know how one could end up in that scenario, maybe we would want to log an error when that occurs? But that might not be necessary as can just be a guard to prevent nil pointer exceptions.

but this must be a thing for unit tests, I don't think  that is possible have a request without the host field set, when you create the RESTClient you have to pass a host or it defaults to localhost ... and the request have the host field immutable 

Is this a real problem?

I don't think so, it was just an oddity I noticed when reviewing https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108396#discussion_r995590210. Since we don't think we will ever encounter this scenario it might not be worth cleaning up.

> Is this a real problem?

i don't think so, in fact I mention this in the description - `the RESTClient.base may never be empty, so the label is never set to none in a real cluster?`
I am closing it, as we agree that this will never be an issue in real clusters

title: CSI migration race condition can cause unexpected detach and data loss
body:
### What happened?

After the cluster was updated to enable PD CSI Driver, there was a race condition where AD Controller (kube-controller-manager) started to [populate the desired state of world](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dc2898b20c6bd9602ae1c3b51333e2e4640ed249/pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/attach_detach_controller.go#L438-L447) BEFORE the PD CSI Driver was up, thus AD Controller gave us the error 

```
Error creating spec for volume "elasticsearch", pod "XXX"/"elasticsearch-0": error performing CSI migration checks and translation for PVC "dXX"/"elasticsearch-elasticsearch-0": in-tree plugin kubernetes.io/gce-pd is migrated on node gke-stage-XXXXX but driver pd.csi.storage.gke.io is not installed.
```

Then AD Controller triggered the disk detach because the disk/volume was not populated in the desired state of world.

Unfortunately the disk was in use during this detach and got corrupted.

### What did you expect to happen?

Since cluster upgrades can cause the controller manager and CSI drivers to start at different times, the AD controller needs to be more conservative when detaching

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We have not been able to reproduce this, it came up from a customer.

### Anything else we need to know?

/sig storage
/assign @mattcary

### Kubernetes version

<details>
k8s 1.23, CSI migration enabled
</details>

I think there's potentially two changes we should do:
1) for the initial DSW population, we should skip the check that if the csi driver is not installed.
2) in general, we should not skip volumes during dsw initial population if an error is returned. If we had some temporary api server error then that would cause volumes to not get added to dsw and similar behavior happen. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dc2898b20c6bd9602ae1c3b51333e2e4640ed249/pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/attach_detach_controller.go#L446

cc @gnufied @jingxu97

@mattcary for a repro, maybe you can try something like:

1. on a cluster with csi migration enabled (control plane + nodes)
1. create a pod with intree-volume and get it running
1. delete the csi driver node daemonset. verify the driver is removed from CSINode
1. restart kube-controller-manager
cc @sunnylovestiramisu

/cc @songjiaxun 

@songjiaxun was trying to repro this, but on GKE with the managed driver which made it complicated.
Yeah maybe gce kube-up would be easier for a repro

If CSINode says that it has migrated GCP PD volume plugin to CSI, then IMO A/D controller should always attach GCP PD volumes to it using CSI, regardless if the CSI driver is present or not. In-tree volume plugin in the kubelet is disabled and can't mount any in-tree volumes anyway.

To flip the migration feature gate / upgrade / downgrade kubelet, the cluster admin must drain the node first to make sure everything is detached. A/D controller should not see change of CSINode migration annotations with any volume attached to it.
/priority important-soon

Another option could be to process these volumes anyways but add them to DSOW with migration status as "uncertain", so as they can be re-processed later.  But surely it looks like @jsafrane might be easiest unless it has any downsides.

There wasn't a node update in this case---there was a control plane update which restarted the PD CSI driver, and it looks like the CSIDriver resource was updated or changed in some way which raced with the kube-controller-manager restart.
Is there anyway we can know if the csi driver is up and running(like a health check ping) before populating DSW?

We use the CSINode registration to determine that. The discussion here I think is concluding that we should not use that as a criteria for adding the volume to DSW. We only need to check that CSI migration is enabled on the node.
+1 we need to be very resilient against races, I think we have to assume a driver is in process of being installed at any point in the AD controller reconcilliation.
/assign sunnylovestiramisu

title: kube-apiserver doesn't reload the kubelet client certificate/key on each logs query
body:
### What happened?

We bootstrap our clusters with kubeadm (through clusterapi), but provide our own end certs to shorten the certificate validity period.

Because of the shortened validity period, we rotate the file-based endcerts frequently. Recently we started noticing that after performing a certificate rotation, usage of `kubectl logs` was failing with

```sh
error: You must be logged in to the server (the server has asked for the client to provide credentials)
```

From there, we looked at the kube-apiserver and kubelet logs and found log lines like the following:

```
"Unable to authenticate the request due to an error" err="verifying certificate SN=<REMOVED>, SKID=<REMOVED>, AKID=<REMOVED> failed: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid: current time 2022-12-17T02:31:09Z is after 2022-12-17T00:16:30Z"
```

So it looks like kube-apiserver didn't reload the new kubelet client certificate. This issue typically goes away if we restart the kube-apiserver container or continue to run `kubectl logs` in a loop.


### What did you expect to happen?

Being able to replace/rotate the kube-apiserver kubelet client certificate/key without causing failure for any logs or node proxy commands/operations.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We were able to get a repro outside of our environment with the following steps.

1. Created a cluster-api cluster on azure with CAPZ using the standard quickstart flow plus some minor tweaks:
- Added ` kubelet-certificate-authority: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt` as an apiserver argument.
- Added ` rotate-server-certificates: "true"` as a kubelet argument.
- Used kubernetes version 1.23.6 and 1.23.15
2. Manually approved the kubelet server certificate csrs using `kubectl certificate approve`
3. In one shell continually ran `kubectl logs` and `kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<NODE_NAME>/proxy/logs`
4. ssh'd into the controlplane node in another shell. ran  `mv /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-kubelet-client.crt /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-kubelet-client.crt.bak` and vice-versa.

From these steps I was able to see `kubectl logs` commands be successful when there was no certificate file and failed when the certificate file was present. Eventually, the kube-apiserver picks up the up-to-date certificate/file.

I don't know the internals here, but it seems like kube-apiserver was using some sort of cached-connection which had the stale certificate.

### Anything else we need to know?

We believe this used to work in kubernetes v1.21 and below. Need to confirm this by spinning up downlevel clusters.

I don't have a strong familiarity with the code but I wonder if it would be possible to use [dynamicClientCert](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/transport/cert_rotation.go#L42) with the kubelet_client. I have this sample commit that seems to fix the issue. https://github.com/zawachte/kubernetes/commit/b4882c7601c27ed5ce562ecf6c2512fdb1496169

title: Kubernetes Jobs API rapid-fire scheduling doesnt honor exponential backoff characteristics
body:
### What happened?

# Problem

The job controller appears to "rapidly reschedule" several pods at the same time (without backing off) which ultimately appears almost like a batch or gang scheduling workflow.  

... This is the opposite of what the job docs say, bc they clearly state :
```
 The back-off limit is set by default to 6. Failed Pods associated with the Job are recreated by the Job controller with an exponential back-off delay (10s, 20s, 40s ...) capped at six minutes.
```
So, rather then, 

- 10, 20, 40, 80 wait times between trying things we are seeing
- 0, 3, 3, 3, 3 second wait times before pods are being retried

This is in the 1.25 release, but not sure if it also happens earlier.  You can see this in the latest kind version. 




### What did you expect to happen?

Jobs wouldnt schedule the same pod at rapid fire intervals

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

# Details 

Thanks to Ryan for this reproducer: 
```
apiVersion: batch/v1

kind: Job

metadata:

  name: backoff-exp

spec:

  backoffLimit: 100

  template:

    spec:

      containers:

        - name: die

          image: ubuntu

          command: [ "/bin/false" ]

          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent

      restartPolicy: Never

```

Now once this is running, you can graph the values like so: 

```
kubectl get pods -o wide | awk '

BEGIN {

    a["d"] = 24*(\

    a["h"] = 60*(\

    a["m"] = 60*(\

    a["s"] = 1)));

  }

  {

    print fx($5); # kubernetes time elapsed in seconds

  }

  function fx(ktym,    f,u,n,t,i) {

    n = split(ktym, f, /[dhms]/, u)

    t = 0

    for (i=1; i<n; i++) {

      t += f[i] * a[u[i]]

    }

    return t

  }

'|sort
```

And youl see a table like this, where the integers below are the AGE OF PODS in SECONDS.  We can see that the pod ages are 3 seconds apart as opposed to (10, 20, 40, 80 ...) or some other exponentiallly increasing number of seconds, apart..... 
```
69

87
90

```

This is broken when the `JobTrackingWithFinalizers` feature gate is enabled. Note that it was disabled and re-enabled before moving to GA:
- enabled by default in v1.23 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/2c1b3fdb5bd109487e47b395f1ca15c63e5663ff#diff-71e3b98f9a6bbf5b8421e26a7ba0c079f397cd8d49abacdad943c66a4f44f03d
- disabled by default from v1.23.9 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109491
- disabled by default in v1.24 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/3b18613be88955e13f8357fb6d73bc1d0e158844
- enabled by default in v1.25 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/a26920b1902dd1d81a203baa4cb9f919db4e015d
- and moved to GA in v1.26 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/4948918155012b24e4b1cf987f831639c6dbaf9c

If the feature gate is disabled, the pods are retried by honoring exponential backoff characteristics.

From a quick glance, there are a few reasons why this happens:

1. Given that the code below is triggered everytime `uncounted != nil`, the queue is made to `forget` the `key`, so we always end up with a backoff of zero.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bb6edfb96b362736a66946ca7d88774aca167cb4/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L869-L884

2. Even if we updated the above code to only trigger if a status update is required and get the right backoff period, we will have the backoff being calculated twice for each pod failure i.e. t'll end up being something like 10, 10, 20, 20, 40, 40, ...

Looking at:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bb6edfb96b362736a66946ca7d88774aca167cb4/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L308-L330

We can end up with a scenario where:
- Pod A fails, triggering a resync. Since the pod has failed, backoff is calculated and applied.
- Finalizer is removed from Pod A and job status is updated.
- We receive the job update event, but the pod informer cache is stale. This triggers a sync.
- We noticed that Pod A has the status `Failed` so the backoff is applied again.

I'll send a PR to fix both the issues.

```
Only a [.spec.template.spec.restartPolicy](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#restart-policy) equal to Always is allowed, which is the default if not specified.
```

code:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/132f29769dfecfc808adc58f756be43171054094/pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go#L148-L150
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/132f29769dfecfc808adc58f756be43171054094/pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go#L354
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/132f29769dfecfc808adc58f756be43171054094/pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go#L738

kubectl explain Deployment/DaemonSet/StatefulSet.spec.template.spec.restartPolicy descriptions can be misleading, perhaps we need to add more descriptions.
/assign

Unfortunately, the documentation comes from the PodSpec object, which those workload types embed and then place additional restrictions on.

It wouldn't be appropriate to put documentation specific to those embedded uses on the PodSpec object.

I've read two issues, [24725](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/24725) and [40908](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/40908).

Although both issue have been marked as closed, and I understand current implementation supports only "Always" for these workload types, like Deployment, I'm not convinced that it should support only “Always". Like many of others, I believe this is a valid request to have restartPolicy as OnFailure or Never.

Unless it's clear why OnFailure/Never shall not be valid for these workload types and the Kubernetes [specification](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.25/#podspec-v1-core) and [explanation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#restart-policy) get updated as well, I personally believe the kubectl explain command is correct, and doesn't need any changes. On the other hand, the support of OnFailure and Never should be added.

As said by the [specification](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.25/#podspec-v1-core), restartPolicy is "`Restart policy for all containers within the pod.`"

My interpretation, this is the policy to restart the containers in the pod, but not the pod itself, even though it's in the pod spec. Let's say one of the containers in the pod completed successfully or with failures, this container may or may not restart depending on this policy. Although I don't understand why not each container has its own restart policy, this pod-wide shared common policy is good enough for most cases.

Anyway, I don't see a problem with the Kubernetes spec, and I disagree with this change request. Please reconsider making a change to the explain command. Thanks!

I now see the documentation for these workload types, such as [Deployment](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#pod-template), saying only `Always` is allowed. However, I don't understand why. Can someone explain that?

title: New takes precedence over old
body:
### What happened?

[source of the issue](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/resourcequota/resource_quota_controller.go)
```
// Sync periodically resyncs the controller when new resources are observed from discovery.
func (rq *Controller) Sync(discoveryFunc NamespacedResourcesFunc, period time.Duration, stopCh <-chan struct{}) {

	oldResources := make(map[schema.GroupVersionResource]struct{})
	wait.Until(func() {

		newResources, err := GetQuotableResources(discoveryFunc)
		if err != nil {
			utilruntime.HandleError(err)

			if discovery.IsGroupDiscoveryFailedError(err) && len(newResources) > 0 {
				// Because only the key of new Resources is used later, it does not matter to overwrite, but this is a hidden danger
				for k, v := range oldResources {
					newResources[k] = v
				}
```

title: cacher watch timeout not handled when it is not ready
body:
### What happened?

In one of our multi tenant cluster, we've observed that all kubelet requests (under `system-nodes` flow schema) eventually started timing out or aborted due to secret watch request occupying all `system` priority level concurrency share. It happened due to our KMS provider was quite latent (& sometimes failing) for brief amount of time. Due to high latency from KMS provider, all the cacher's reflector list & watch calls start failing (repeatedly retried) and cacher was marked as not ready.

Now all the watch request to the cacher was waiting for `ready` conditional variable and never timed out. This led all watch requests stuck in priority and fairness queue for ever & eventually occupying all the concurrency shares, affecting other requests belonging to same priority level.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f173d01c011c3574dea73a6fa3e20b0ab94531bb/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L457-L467

We need to handle watch timeout when cacher not ready to fix the issue.

### What did you expect to happen?

Watch requests to get time out eventually when cacher is not ready.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Consider a large cluster (5K nodes) having more than 50K number of secret resources encrypted using KMS provider and mounted by various pods in the cluster. Restart api server & artificially induce high latency on KMS provider (assuming we've configured lower dek cache size of 10 items) and wait for kubelet requests to start failing.

### Anything else we need to know?

May we can implement a way to timeout ready conditional variable (sync.Cond) `wait` function. Let me know if I can raise a pull request to fix this. Roughly along below lines:
```go
type ready struct {
	sync.RWMutex

	ok bool
	c chan struct{}
}

func newReady() *ready {
	return &ready{c: make(chan struct{}, 0)}
}

func (r *ready) wait() {
	r.waitChan(nil)
}

func (r *ready) waitChan(stop <-chan struct{}) {
	r.RLock()
	ok, c := r.ok, r.c
	r.RUnlock()
	if ok {
		return
	}
	select {
	case <-stop:
	case <-c:
	}
}

// TODO: Make check() function more sophisticated, in particular
// allow it to behave as "waitWithTimeout".
func (r *ready) check() bool {
	r.RLock()
	defer r.RUnlock()
	return r.ok
}

func (r *ready) set(ok bool) {
	r.Lock()
	r.ok = ok
	close(r.c) // broadcast
	r.c = make(chan struct{})
	r.Unlock()
}
```

@wojtek-t This issue can also occur on CRDs with broken conversion strategies which prevents the apiserver watch-cache from initializing. If I create a CRD with a broken conversion webhook, the apiserver will continually try to initialize its cache on this object type:
```
E0207 22:20:05.623771 11 cacher.go:424] cacher (*unstructured.Unstructured): unexpected ListAndWatch error: failed to list stable.example.com/v1beta1, Kind=CronTab: conversion webhook for stable.example.com/v1, Kind=CronTab failed: Post "https://crd-conversion-webhook.crd-conversion-webhook.svc:443/crdconvert?timeout=30s": service "crd-conversion-webhook" not found; reinitializing...
```
We can list the v1 but not v1beta1 version of this CRD:
```
kubectl get --raw "/apis/stable.example.com/v1beta1/namespaces/default/crontabs"
Error from server: conversion webhook for stable.example.com/v1, Kind=CronTab failed: Post "https://crd-conversion-webhook.crd-conversion-webhook.svc:443/crdconvert?timeout=30s": service "crd-conversion-webhook" not found
```
If we issue a watch against this CRD, we can make requests get stuck inflight indefinitely which can max out the given PriorityLevelConfiguration:
```
# Make this request 5 times
kubectl get --raw "/apis/stable.example.com/v1beta1/namespaces/default/crontabs?watch=true"
^C

# Check executing requests for global-default and we see 5 stuck watch requests
$ kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_flowcontrol_current_executing_requests | grep global-default
apiserver_flowcontrol_current_executing_requests{flow_schema="global-default",priority_level="global-default"} 5
```
Even if we close the watch connection, the request is still counted as an executing request. I confirmed this issue is still present in v1.25.6. The mitigation for this is to delete or fix the problematic CRD but it looks like an apiserver restart is the only way to recover from this if the given PriorityLevelConfiguration has reached it's maximum concurrency. I can share a reproduction for this if needed.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115656 should fix this problem

title: Multiple EBS PVCs in one pod can be bound to PVs in different AZs
body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


#### What happened:

I am creator of https://github.com/plumber-cd/kubernetes-dynamic-reclaimable-pvc-controllers and its README will tell exactly what I am trying to achieve there and why, but the bottom line - I have multiple EBS backed storage classes and multiple PVs in these storage classes with the status `Available`. If I create multiple PVCs (one per each storage class) to be mounted in one pod - it seems to randomly grab and bind to existing PVs even if these PVs might happen to be in different AZs. Even though I had my storage classes set to `WaitForFirstConsumer` - but I guess it did waited for the first consumer, it just didn't waited for it to be scheduled to a node. This seems to happen on 1.15 and 1.17 (didn't test other versions).

#### What you expected to happen:

I'd expect PVCs to bind to PVs in the same AZ when they're owned by the same pod. Ideally the pod needs to land on a node first, then PVCs would need to grab PVs in the node's AZ - but I am not sure if it's possible to schedule the pod while it's volumes can't be mounted.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

1. Create two storage classes backed by EBS
2. Create two PVs per each class in different AZs and make sure they are `Available`
3. Create two PVCs per each class and a pod that mounts them

#### Anything else we need to know?:

My suspicion is that normally EBS provisioner will take care of matching AZ, but since there is no PV provisioning happening here and PVCs trying to grab existing PVs - why it fails.

#### Environment:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.17.17
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: AWS
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`): flatcar 2765.2.6
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): 5.10.43-flatcar
- Install tools: kops
- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug): calico
- Others: brain, hands

title: Auto-closing issues is harmful and causes friction
body:
Previously open issue : https://github.com/kubernetes/community/issues/5473
Twitter Discussion : https://twitter.com/BenTheElder/status/1407774856033181696

There's pros and cons to having a bot do this, let me try to enumerate current situation here:
- maintainers don't have to play bad cop
- keep set of open issues at a maintainable level
- bot commands are available to org members to `/reopen` reduces friction
- lifecycle labels help folks specify which issues not to touch
- we currently do not have dedicated team(s) that do issue triage well (except for some SIG like api-machinery that do this really well with twice a week triage session)
- initial issue labeling is still a problem, routing issues to the correct sig
- we have a new triage label which is not widely used yet across sigs

However there are numerous problems with the current situation:
- impression that project does not care about bugs
- folks open new issues for things that may be already present but closed
- too much traffic/noise from the bot activity
- issues where some follow up was requested/needed gets closed 

Options to do better?
- triage party 
- more hands on deck, train incoming folks to do issue triage and manage that as a subproject of some SIG
- stop the bot cold and let the SIGs adjust

What did i miss @BenTheElder ?

/sig contributor-experience

PS: It will be ironic if this issue gets auto-closed!

nodes.body:
@dims: This issue is currently awaiting triage.

If a SIG or subproject determines this is a relevant issue, they will accept it by applying the `triage/accepted` label and provide further guidance.

The `triage/accepted` label can be added by org members by writing `/triage accepted` in a comment.


<details>

Instructions for interacting with me using PR comments are available [here](https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/pull-requests.md).  If you have questions or suggestions related to my behavior, please file an issue against the [kubernetes/test-infra](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/issues/new?title=Prow%20issue:) repository.
</details>

It seems like a good idea to revisit the workflows here. What follows is very much my opinion and not representing any SIG. It also covers more than just autoclose.

Auto close _does_ avoid issues piling up.

- I'm OK with the idea of never closing issues that are triaged as accepted
- I'm also OK with the idea of auto closing issues that have been marked as needs more information or as support, and haven't had a response since they were so labelled.
- I'd be interested in splitting the “backlog” priority level into “stuff we'd clearly like to do as a SIG, and would if there were resources” vs. “it's a valid suggestion but it'll only happen if someone takes it forward”. For an example of the latter see issue 25061 in k/website: *Allow switching website between “light mode” and “dark mode”*.
- That split would help us let things fall off the second backlog, but perhaps let them stay on the first.
- Priorities above backlog should not autoclose, but I do want to see them rot and then be labelled _something_ if we don't get to them. Maybe become “overdue” or “unaddressed”?

For k/website, issues that haven't been triaged in _n_ days could go straight to _unaddressed_, skipping stale and rotten.
Does https://github.com/features/issues provide any new way to track issues and help avoid closing ones that are worth keeping?

I want to point out that while the original somewhat hyperbolic tweet took off far beyond expectation there is an important follow-up: https://twitter.com/bentheelder/status/1407906836175491076

IMHO the biggest issue we have is staffing problems keeping after triage and so on.

> more hands on deck, train incoming folks to do issue triage and manage that as a subproject of some SIG

Perhaps a new role in SIGs recognizing the folks that do issue triage? I think we need some way to recognize and encourage doing this, in addition to some workflow guidance or tooling (such as triage-party instances).

Bot noise impacts me a lot, personally. To keep something like KIND running well @ Kubernetes HEAD + manage SIG testing etc. I am subscribed to a lot of issues and a *huge* amount of comments are just the lifecycle robot and users fending it off.
Frozen issues are cheaper, they see little noise when nobody is working on them and IMHO if these issues are breaking triage workflows then the workflows need to be improved.

But as mentioned above I think the important part is that this harms the reputation of the project immensely because for many people their first interaction is filing a bug or PR that slips through the cracks and then gets harassed by the auto close bot. We have other people exasperated and futilely commenting every time the bot comments to undo it. There is a sub thread about folks who outright said they do not participate anymore after this experience. Once we burn those folks they don't come back.

I think closing issues we never got to hides just how many of those exist except from those in the know about querying the right labels.

> I'd be interested in splitting the “backlog” priority level into “stuff we'd clearly like to do as a SIG, and would if there were resources” vs. “it's a valid suggestion but it'll only happen if someone takes it forward”. For an example of the latter see issue 25061 in k/website: Allow switching website between “light mode” and “dark mode”.

I think this would be useful signaling regardless.

> I'm also OK with the idea of auto closing issues that have been marked as needs more information or as support, and haven't had a response since they were so labelled.

I would add that we should consider poking for information (the bot could do this) at some point in the lifecycle.

+1, there's a big difference between we can't move forward with the issue because the author is not responding and we need information and the issue not getting a response from us. Auto-closing this sort of issue seems unlikely to produce the same response and keeping them open seems unlikely to net much for anyone.

In general +1 to @sftims comment above.

It's worth noting that most of our repos are not kubernetes/kubernetes scale and even a moderately busy repo is probably already more doable to triage without this than our busiest repos, I think we have two different scales of problems but we bluntly apply one workflow org wide.

We are trying disabling it on the KIND repo, which seems to clearly fall into the latter scale.

One thing we're going to start experimenting with in Knative is building an issue-triage report to make this sort of thing more manageable:

The initial focus will be simply on quantifying the bot impact:

How many issues touched in the last 100 days:
* Were marked by the stale-bot?
* And had a human undo the stale-bot?
* First item and never had an org member comment?

If there's interest, it might also be possible to collect org member stats on issue replies (maybe treating first and last specially). This could help highlight people who are doing a great job of triage and issue-closing.

Being mostly on the user side I do feel a lot of frustration with these. I think auto-closing specifically in the case of a ticket/PR being in a "waiting for OP to respond" state is okay but when the issue is accepted as real and there's nothing more to say, then auto-closing them is pretty grumble-inducing. Auto-closing untriaged tickets/PRs feels like a gray area, can see both sides, and probably should be a special case and a sign that our triage process needs improvement.

This reminds me of the different types of strategies used by dictionaries. Some are descriptive -- describing how people use words -- whereas others are prescriptive -- informing people how they should use words. 

https://www.merriam-webster.com/words-at-play/descriptive-vs-prescriptive-defining-lexicography

What strategy should we use for the backlog of issues that no one has engaged with in half a decade?
* prescriptive  -- this issue is still probably broken and someone still ought to fix it
* descriptive -- no one has or will work on this issue, close it so it doesn't distract from the things we are fixing.

Neither is correct per se. Although I would note that most dictionaries these days tend to be descriptive.

Ideally we can figure out how to redirect the energy spent getting angry at automated descriptive processes and towards fixing more issues more consistently.

> impression that project does not care about bugs

The impression that the project does not care about bugs is an accurate conclusion implied by the large number of auto-closed issues. At the very least, the project's ability to generate bugs is higher than the community's current ability to fix them.

Pulling the battery out of a smoke detector is unlikely to put out a fire.

> [auto-closing bugs] harms the reputation of the project immensely because for many people their first interaction is filing a bug or PR that slips through the cracks and then gets harassed by the auto close bot. We have other people exasperated and futilely commenting every time the bot comments to undo it. 

In the same way smoke detectors rarely cause fires, I would not assign the cause of the reputational harm from ignoring bugs to automated processes that flag things as ignored.

Rather I would note the lack of the right processes in place that allow the maintainers on this project respond to incoming issues faster than they are supplied and also identify issues that have fallen through the cracks.

> What strategy should we use for the backlog of issues that no one has engaged with in half a decade?

We close bugs _far_ quicker than half a decade. IMO the amount of time a bug spends open is actually immaterial. If the bug is real and not fixed it deserves to be tracked, it is wasteful to file N bugs for the same problem, and it prevents users from tracking resolution when we spread it out in this way.

We've yet to have any solid arguments as to why open bugs are harmful. At best there is some complaint about issue triage, but that is accomplishable with e.g. just labeling the issue and filtering by label. Closing is orthogonal.

> Ideally we can figure out how to redirect the energy spent getting angry at automated descriptive processes and towards fixing more issues more consistently.

Many people filing bugs are ill equipped to fix them. A user of the project may not be in the right position / experience to resolve a bug. Their frustration is still relevant to the success of the project. There is also a lot of energy wasted in `/remove-lifecycle` comments.

> The impression that the project does not care about bugs is an accurate conclusion implied by the large number of auto-closed issues. At the very least, the project's ability to generate bugs is higher than the community's current ability to fix them.

Not even leaving the bug tracked and dismissively closing it is a bit different than not getting to it.

> In the same way smoke detectors rarely cause fires, I would not assign the cause of the reputational harm from ignoring bugs to automated processes that flag things as ignored.

There is explicitly evidence that there is reputational harm from this. Off hand: https://twitter.com/jordansissel/status/1407857648083472388
"K8s auto closing bot is why I don’t interact with k8s projects anymore. 😭👍🏻"

Further, I'd say this is not comparable to a smoke detector. Tracking the amount of inactive bugs is a smoke detector.
Closing them actually obscures this, I'd have a different impression encountering a project with ~9k bugs open than < 2k. How many people are aware of searching github for the closed issues with special label?

Closing issues is more like having a robot dump the flaming objects in your backyard so the smoke detector stops going off.

> Rather I would note the lack of the right processes in place that allow the maintainers on this project respond to incoming issues faster than they are supplied and also identify issues that have fallen through the cracks.

This is almost certainly the most important thing to address. That doesn't mean that other aspects of the current approach aren't problematic though.

> Tracking the amount of inactive bugs is a smoke detector.

How would you separate active from inactive bugs?

> Their frustration is still relevant to the success of the project. There is also a lot of energy wasted in /remove-lifecycle comments.

Both of these are good signals that a SIG has underinvested in their triage or development process and/or have other problems (bad design/impl causing problems, important unhandled use cases, etc).

> How would you separate active from inactive bugs?

Auto-Labeling + search queries used by triagers or triage tooling still seems potentially relevant, but less heavy handed.

> Both of these are good signals that a SIG has underinvested in their triage or development process and/or have other problems (bad design/impl causing problems, important unhandled use cases, etc).

Yes -- we definitely have signal that triage processes are under-staffed / optimized / not going well, and it is definitely not uniform across SIGs (some are doing quite well).

As for how we might improve that, https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-testing/issues/7 is one issue tracking exploring that.

So people don't have to wade through Twitter, let me summarize my 2c...

Volume:

- We have nearly 7000 issues in k/k closed with the rotten label; realistically that's over 1000/yr: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed+label%3Alifecycle%2Frotten
- On average for the past year, we have 35 new issues opened every day: https://k8s.devstats.cncf.io/d/39/issues-opened-closed-by-sig?orgId=1&var-period=d&var-repo_name=kubernetes%2Fkubernetes&var-repo=kuberneteskubernetes&var-sig_name=All&var-kind_name=All
- From experience with SIG Instrumentation, I estimate that we typically triage about 5 issues per 30m session. I think it's therefore reasonable to estimate that one person could easily fill an entire half of their workday just triaging incoming issues to k/k, 7 days a week.

Contributor and issue filer expectations:

- Allowing a backlog of issues that anyone can file to grow forever fails to set healthy boundaries and realistic expectations around support in a FOSS project. Closed, stale issues illustrates the staffing gap and at least shifts some of the emotional labor on closing stale issues (which no one enjoys doing!! particularly if the reply that comes back is rude!) to a bot.
- I think there's a difference between closing issues that have been confirmed at some point but we're not staffed to handle vs. various user support requests, perhaps where the reporter is unresponsive.
- I frequently struggle with confirmed, legitimate issues that the project doesn't have resources to address, because there are only so many things we can prioritize working on. Even if an outside contributor does the work to fix the problem, reviewer/approver time is very limited.
- Addressing the limited approver time gap is not easy. It is extremely challenging to develop the experience to apply for approver on some of the high volume areas of the codebase (API Machinery, Node, etc.) You need to work on the project full-time, and that requires funding/employment. Many areas of the project have a lottery factor of 1.

At the moment, I think it's clear that SIGs are not resourced to manage the current volume of incoming issues in k/k. I think it's also fair to argue that the stale bot has discouraged issue filing, so I suspect that if we staffed the project for current issue load, we could easily see it increase in a short time and would find ourselves understaffed again.

Could the project hire someone to do full-time issue triage and management? And, if we did this, would we have sufficient staffing in SIGs to manage the workload of legitimate bugs and feature requests after moving the bottleneck?

FWIW:
- the way the comments are done right now is via a commenter tool that comments on anything matching a certain github query
- it's super boilerplate-heavy and not able to be concisely configured in a way that would allow certain repos to opt-opt, or configure different thresholds, or different lifecycles, etc.
- if someone wanted to invest the effort in writing a purpose-built lifecycle management tool, this would probably be way easier to accomplish

I feel like with the possible exception of kubernetes/kubernetes, it would be super cool to use a default that is selectively overridable by specific subprojects or SIGs.

As to effectiveness, I don't know anyone who's bothered to gather data on:
- whether perma-unstaling issues has been effective in getting them addressed (aka is this an alternate way of people spamming +1 or :thumbsup: on the issue to vote? does anyone pay attention?)
- whether auto-closed issues resurface later as larger-impact / higher-priority issues (aka we could have saved ourselves pain if we had addressed it earlier)

What would be a friendlier way to express that there isn't sufficient contributor capacity to even look at a given issue / PR? 

How would folks propose increasing contributor capacity to ensure that all issues / PRs can be looked at?

> it's super boilerplate-heavy and not able to be concisely configured in a way that would allow certain repos to opt-opt, or configure different thresholds, or different lifecycles, etc.

Overall I would agree that this is true but opt-out entirely is not really problematic, we're piloting this on the KIND repo.

You can see the three line diff necessary here: 
https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/22675/files

> if someone wanted to invest the effort in writing a purpose-built lifecycle management tool, this would probably way easier to accomplish

I don't think anyone needs to alter the tool to support this or alternate per-repo comments, the tool is flexible and uses github search parameters for choosing where to comment. GitHub search is well documented and plenty powerful enough to exclude and include specific projects.

> What would be a friendlier way to express that there isn't sufficient contributor capacity to even look at a given issue / PR?

At the very least the phrasing can be a bit less blunt / more helpful, see also https://github.com/knative/community/issues/665#issuecomment-873873770, https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/issues/22911

Marking issues as needing triage and a perhaps a comment explaining the limited bandwidth etc. seems more useful than people `/remove-lifecycle`ing for years.

> How would folks propose increasing contributor capacity to ensure that all issues / PRs can be looked at?

I don't think you have to address that issue to resolve that the current approach to closing them out is noisy and frustrating.

Resolving capacity is not something people can solve with their own time and efforts, we need more staffed contributors, which at most we can raise to our employers.

I think we can reduce the issue count differently however:

We should also probably consider entirely removing / auto-closing the feature type in favor of asking people to file KEPs. And also the support type. Realistically most of the time we are manually re-pointing these issues to the the enhancements rep and the forums respectively, which could be automated, leaving only bugs, flaking/failing tests to deal with.

It is perhaps worth noting that this is factoring into the decision to donate kube-rs into the project https://github.com/kube-rs/kube-rs/issues/584, there should probably be a discussion somewhere (else?) about formally allowing subprojects to opt out of this. 

Previously we refused at least one project's request (helm, as I recall), though we've since (unofficially?) permitted merging this for one project (KIND, see above).

> We close bugs far quicker than half a decade

I know that in k/website / SIG Docs we struggle to make improvements even when they've been _marked_ as important for some time. https://github.com/kubernetes/website/issues/4322 springs to mind. Folks are chipping away at the pile of frozen issues that have ended up at the end of the far end of the list.

Automatic closure has “helped” by making those frozen issues stand out. However, there's definitely a risk that some good idea never made it past triage and disappeared into the pile of closed suggestions.

I wanted to add a good example which IMHO shouldn't be auto-closed:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/7890 is the [the top 5 of all upvoted issues](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+sort%3Areactions-%2B1-desc) but it is/was scheduled by the bot to be autoclosed.

> Previously we refused at least one project's request (helm, as I recall),

Can confirm it was the Helm project (@spiffxp and I chatted about this at the first Helm Summit).

>Can confirm it was the Helm project (@spiffxp and I chatted about this at the first Helm Summit).

*takes sip from helm summit water bottle* that was a fun summit

If there was an outright denial I sure hope it didn't come from me, though maybe I was the messenger.  At the time I think the project was trying to tamp down the entropy of every repo having different rules of engagement.  Onboard a contributor to the project, and they should be capable of contributing to any of our 200+ repos.  The bot was a way of maintaining some kind of expectation that issues that haven't been touched in 150 days are implicitly deemed as not urgent enough to work on.

I personally am totally fine with repos that wish to exclude themselves from this workflow, with the exception of kubernetes/kubernetes.  That said I ultimately think this is a SIG Contributor Experience call.

As a maintainer, personally, I'd want to concentrate on

And other than issues that lack info and don't receive more info after some time, all issues are considered accepted without the triage labeling.

nodes.title: Don't auto-close triaged issues, require re-triage after 1yr
nodes.body:
Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/103151

This PR makes the following workflow changes (separate commits):
1. **Don't auto-close triaged issues, don't mark triaged issues as stale/rotten** - Triaged issues have already been vetted by an org member as being relevant and having sufficient information. By ignoring triaged issues for lifecycle changes, this should reduce a lot of unnecessary churn & friction for maintainers.
2. **Require issues to be retriaged when untouched for a set amount of time** - This essentially adds a new lifecycle stage with a much greater (1 year vs 90 days) window. The idea is that the project changes a lot in 1 year, and it makes sense for issues that have been untouched for that amount of time to be retriaged, to ensure they are still relevant. Note that once the triage label is removed, the regular stale/rotten/closed lifecycle checks kick back in.
    - `critical-urgent` - retriage after 30 days of inactivity
    - `important-soon` - retriage after 90 days of inactivity
    - `important-longterm` and `backlog` - retriage after 1 year of inactivity
3. **Don't auto-close important issues** - Issues labeled with `priority/critical-urgent`, `priority/important-soon` or `priority/important-longterm` will no longer be auto-closed from the `lifecycle/rotten` state.
4. **Remove the job that marks important triaged issues as frozen** - This is redundant with the changes in (1) and (3).

/hold
for comment

/sig contributor-experience

title: Validation fails for CustomResource with array of pointers
body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**:

I have a CustomResourceDefinition with a schema that includes an array property, where each element of the array is either an integer or null. This is implemented in the CRD like so:

```
spec:
  properties:
    allocations:
      items:
        nullable: true
        type: integer
      type: array
```

Using the golang client, I am able to properly write instances of the custom resource. However, `kubectl` fails validation with the following error when attempting to edit an instance of the custom resource:

>  ValidationError(IPAMBlock.spec.allocations): unknown object type "nil" in IPAMBlock.spec.allocations[3]

This error is duplicated for each "null" entry in the "allocations" array. This can be reproduced simply by using `kubectl edit` on a resource created by the golang client, and then saving the resource with no changes. It seems to be a problem with kubectl validation, since `kubectl edit --validate=false` successfully updates the resource (but hits this other bug instead: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/98080).

**What you expected to happen**:

I can modify the custom resource using kubectl without errors or turning off validation.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

I encountered this in the context of Calico. If you have a cluster running Calico, you should be able to hit this with the following command:

```
kubectl edit ipamblocks
```

Then, simply save without changing anything.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
- 
```
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"18", GitVersion:"v1.18.8", GitCommit:"9f2892aab98fe339f3bd70e3c470144299398ace", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2020-08-13T16:12:48Z", GoVersion:"go1.13.15", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"18", GitVersion:"v1.18.2", GitCommit:"52c56ce7a8272c798dbc29846288d7cd9fbae032", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2020-04-30T20:19:45Z", GoVersion:"go1.13.9", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
```

@liggitt was also able to reproduce on master.

CC @sttts @soltysh 

/sig api-machinery

title: Create ability to do zero downtime deployments when using externalTrafficPolicy: Local
body:
I am using externalTrafficPolicy set to Local for my a LoadBalancer service for an ingress controller on GKE.

Right now, when a pod gets terminated, it is immediately removed from the NodePort service, which stops traffic from routing to the pod (step 5 at https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod/#termination-of-pods). 

The problem is that the GCP Load Balancer doesn't update itself immediately, so it continues to send traffic to the NodePort even though Kubernetes has already removed the pod from the NodePort as part of the termination process. This results in timeouts and an inability to do zero downtime deployments when a node no longer has an active application residing on it when externalTrafficPolicy is set to Local.

I'd like to see an option where we can use Local, but allow for zero-downtime deployments. 

I'm wondering if there could be a configurable option to wait until a preStop hook has finished (or grace period hits) before removing the pod from the NodePort service? With something like this, we could make a preStop hook that can make health checks fail but have the pod continue to serve traffic normally. The preStop hook could then sleep for a certain amount of time while the load balancers gracefully stop sending traffic because the health checks start to fail. Once the preStop hook completes, then it removes the pod from the NodePort. This would allow for graceful draining of outgoing pods.

Or maybe the answer is a pre-PreStop hook that can run before termination officially begins?

Having the same issue. Any graceful termination in the pod itself will not help, since the port at node level stop accepting traffic.

Same issue here. I tried to fix in a few months ago but gave up in the end and set `externalTrafficPolicy` to `Cluster` (loosing the client ip but deploy zero-downtime). The issue is that the Google LBs don't get a signal BEFORE a pod is terminated, so only after the not configurable healthcheck timeout the node is deregistered from the LB. Found no way so far to remove the node from the LB before terminating the POD.

This is a problem with 2-hop load-balancing - the end-of-life handling of pods doesn't really have a way to describe "upstream" dependencies and sequencing.  The endpoints controller sees the pod as terminating and immediately removes it from the set.  Kube-proxy has no choice but to also remove it from the list of available backends.  As you described, the upstream LB hasn't received the news yet.

For HTTP apps, If you use Ingress and VPC-Native LB (on GCP) you will bypass this second hop (kube-proxy) and the LB goes directly to the pod.  During the terminationGracePeriod, the pod will be removed from the LB.

For apps that use Service, this remains a problem.  I'd like this to be possible.  It probably needs a KEP to cover the details, but maybe something like:

* Instead of removing a terminating endpoint, move it to NotReadyAddresses
* In kube-proxy, if a service has no viable ready endpoints, but has not-ready addresses, use those

For "local" services that would still use the terminating endpoint.  Presumably, upstream LBs would be deconfigured and incoming traffic would taper off.

That doesn't seem egregiously complicated to me, but I bet there are corner cases.  Here's one - NotReady covers both startup and teardown.  Would we want LBs to go to not-yet-initialized backends at the beginning of life?  It seems wrong but not terribly so.  Here's another - it will add a lot of endpoints writes as we have to process both states.

@freehan @robscott

I don't have much to add here, agree that it would likely take a KEP to completely solve this. One may already be in the works that could help. Although this primarily has IPVS in mind, the proposed API change here could likely help solve this issue as well: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/1607.

I am also dealing with this same issue.

The approach I had in mind was another option for `externalTrafficPolicy`  My thought was...  What if in addition to `Local` and `Cluster` there was something like a `LocalBeforeCluster` or `ClusterButPreferLocal`  where the behavior would always prefer a local pod, and retain the ability to preserve client IP when the traffic is local.  But as a fallback, it would bounce the traffic to other Pods in the cluster if the local one isn't available.

With this "solution" the load balancer would never really detect a problem, during normal ingress controller updates, but it would if there was a more serious problem going on at the node.

I'm sure there's some sort of gotcha in how the service routing works that might make it impossible to have it both ways, but figured I would mention this angle as well.

The "gotcha" is that "Local" changes the way traffic is routed to endpoints
(removes SNAT) and so that behavior (which is very visible to the serving
Pod) would be conditional on whether endpoints exist.  That's kind of
unpleasant.

Rob's xref to https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/1607 is
exactly right - I think these two together could work nicely.  I wonder if
we can link them up.  Needs an implementor.
