@WillPlatnick 

This is not a solution to the root cause, but I've been working on an approach that is proving to work out pretty nicely for me.    I have the same exact use case as you.  I want to be able to update my ingress controllers without experiencing any downtime due to load balancer health check lag.

In my case I'm using the nginx-ingress controller, and I'm using the stable/nginx-ingress helm chart to deploy it.   Some key settings are:

- DaemonSet
- `Service` with `type: NodePort` and `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`

My solution is to run TWO DaemonSets.  The two DaemonSets have matching selector/labels, so that they are ALL fronted by the same Service.

With this setup, all I have to do is just ensure that redeployments happen to only one DaemonSet at a time to avoid a situation where a particular node fails to have any running ingress-controller pods.

To facilitate this, what i've prototyped are some changes to the helm chart that make it possible for me to have two separate helm releases.  The first helm release deploys a daemonset, service, configmap.  The second helm release deploys another daemonset, but skips the service and configmap and ensures that the daemonset's labels match those of the first release.

I've also played around with the idea of a single helm release, that has the extra daemonset.  Howwever, with that approach, I think it would be more dificult to do ingress controller upgrades, since the two helm release approach allows me to update the helm chart on ONE before the OTHER.

Regarding that last statement I made above.  I do think the single helm chart is viable, because I think that a pod disruption policy that applies to both daemonsets simultaneously could be used to ensure that never more than one pod is out at a time.

Edit: I don't know if this will work the way I was hoping.  Seems like PodDisruptionBudgets don't work with DaemonSets the way I thought they would.  

Ideally to make my double daemonset approach work, I would like to be able to have a PDB who's selectors match both daemonsets, but limit the max unavailable to 1.  Forcing a redeployment to only impact one pod at a time.

Clever.  The proposal to keep "terminating" endpoints would give you the
same behavior, I think.

This issue also causes a problem just using HPA for ingress-nginx with externalTrafficPolicy: Local and the GCP Load Balancer. If there is a spike in traffic that causes the deployment to scale up, it means we will very often see traffic timing out once the traffic dies down and HPA scales down those pods, assuming it happened to be the last pod on a node. The healthCheckNodePort response correctly reports an error status code as soon as the pod begins terminating, but the actual port serving traffic closes immediately even though there is a long preStop delay before the pod actually terminates.

As a mitigation, I've tried running both a Deployment and DaemonSet to ensure at least one pod on each node; the problem is that the DaemonSet pod can be even more dangerous, since it can drop the connection in the middle of a long-running request if the node itself is being terminated.

Any alternative strategies would be welcome here -- the biggest concern is being able to retain the remote IP (for geolocation), and being able to potentially scale the ingress controller dramatically based on spiky traffic. So far, the only viable option seems to be to move to Google's L7 proxy, but that would mean the loss of several features we currently depend on. In the meantime, our only choice seems to be to massively overprovision the deployment and disable HPA.

title: Investigate callers of IsLikelyNotMountPoint
body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!-->


**What happened**:
IsLikelyNotMountPoint() doesn't detect bind mounts of directories on the same fs as /var/lib/kubelet.  Local PVs that are directories on the rootfs are most problematic.  Similar CSI plugins that expose rootfs directories are also problematic. 

[This commit](https://github.com/msau42/kubernetes/commit/559fdd5229eb550054df57d1854d58dc4cd7c506) identifies some functions that are technically incorrect because they use IsLikelyNotMountPoint() instead of IsNotMountPoint().  However, IsNotMountPoint() is expensive since it has to scan all mount points on the host, so instead of changing the callers to use IsNotMountPoint(), we found other ways to fix the problem.

We should investigate all other uses of IsLikelyNotMountPoint() to see if these cases are handled.

@kubernetes/sig-storage-bugs 

<!-- DO NOT EDIT BELOW THIS LINE -->
/kind bug

nodes.body: Here's another place where IsLikelyNotMountPoint() needs to change: https://sourcegraph.com/github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/-/blob/pkg/volume/csi/csi_mounter.go#L387

hmm, it has been documented that `IsLikelyNotMountPoint` does not ALWAYS return correct information, esp. about bind mounts - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/util/mount/mount_linux.go#L241

I guess the intent was to use it for volume types that expose a new devices and not to use it for detecting mount points which are basically bind mounts of local directories onto rootfs itself.   For local storage it is a problem if admin ended up adding rootfs device to local-storage pool. 

For many use cases it is possibly to flip the switch via https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/util/util.go#L131

If we do want to check mount table each time we want to really verify if a directory is a mount point then we should investigate poll based interface @cofyc implemented awhile back for polling the mount table. That may be cheaper than querying mount table all the time.

Yes, we should investigate all calls to IsLikelyNotMountPoint() that's in the general volume manager code (not plugin-specific), as well as CSI logic.  We have to evaluate the performance implications since IsNotMountPoint is more expensive.

The other thing I've been thinking, is to evaluate in each case if we even need to check if something is a mount point?  If you try to `os.Remove` a mount point or directory with content, it will fail.
xref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/72257
/assign

title: Service.Spec.ExternalIPs should not allow duplication
body:
/kind feature


**What happened**: Accidentally created two distinct services with the same `externalip:port` combination. This creates a race where one of the services, on a per-node basis, becomes unavailable.

**What you expected to happen**: An error from the service validation, same as trying to allocate a duplicate `clusterIP`

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**: Create two services with a duplicate port and service ip:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  externalIPs: ["172.17.0.1"]
  ports:
    - name: web
      port: 80
  selector:
    app: nginx
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service

  name: nginx2
```

I'm pretty sure this is a bug.

The only possible use I can imagine for this would be if there were some ordering constraint when the externalIP were bound such that the creation date of the first service always won.  That way you could define the second service and later remove the first to cut over seamlessly.  Otherwise there might be a tiny gap in availability.

However, I don't believe that the ordering is respected.

I looked at this one, here is a little background some probably already know about:

**Current behavior on the node**
If two services used the same externalIP:port, kube-proxy will setup iptables rules twice for the same externalIP:port. So traffic will be redirected to the endpoints of the service that was processed first.


**Validation**
In the case where ClusterIP is provided in the service spec, the check for whether it was allocated or not is done through the [ClusterIP allocator](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d6c8edd391d15b03aa9e79c39ed7036b6a379a6b/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/rest.go#L621), since ClusterIPs come from a predefined limited range, the allocator represents its state in memory as a bitmap, persisted in etcd.

We can't use the same range allocator to track externalIPs since they don't come from a predefined range, let alone that we need to also track which ports were allocated per externalIP, and so we need a different setup to track what externalIP:port already allocated, an explicit map persisted in etcd.

Agree with @ahg-g - we can't do synchronous validation of this, and I don't think we'd want to.

We could define what happens when you do this (e.g. the Service with the oldest CreationTimestamp wins) but even that seems like realllllly diminishing returns.

My inclination is to close this as "working as intended" but I want to here if anyone thinks the stable-sort behavior is worth the effort.  Keep in mind we have not just in-tree implementations, so this becomes a tax on them all.
Perhaps we just document that using duplicate externalIPs results in undefined behavior.

It's really not different than if you set the status of 2 services to have
the same LB IP

title: service.alpha.kubernetes.io/tolerate-unready-endpoints misuses the Endpoints API object
body:
**BUG REPORT**: The [addEndpointSubset method](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/endpoint/endpoints_controller.go#L509-L528) of the endpoints controller is currently adding EndpointSubsets with Address that are unready base on the `service.alpha.kubernetes.io/tolerate-unready-endpoints` annotation. 

At a minimum those addresses need to be added as EndpointSubsets with UnreadyAddresses, and the decision on whether to add them should be made, based on the annotation or its equivalent field, in the default DNS implementation's [handleEndpointUpdate](https://github.com/kubernetes/dns/blob/master/pkg/dns/dns.go#L320-L381) and [generateRecordsforHeadlessService](https://github.com/kubernetes/dns/blob/master/pkg/dns/dns.go#L480-L520) methods.

We might also consider simply always creating SRV records without respect to readiness. That is, the DNS implementation could disregard readiness for the endpoints associated with a headless services when creating SRV records and only worry about readiness when creating A records. However, if we consider this approach, we might want to give careful thought to what we might break.

Before proceeding with the implementation of either, I'd like to get feedback (and maybe participation) from SIG Network. Particularly as some clusters may not use the kube-dns add-on. I'd like to fix this in the 1.8 - 1.9 time frame if possible.

 /kind bug

nodes.body: /assign @kow3ns

/sig apps
/sig network
@bgrant0607 @smarterclayton @kargakis @janetkuo
@kubernetes/sig-network-bugs
I assume statefulset want kube-dns create A record for headless service even if pod is unready?@bprashanth @foxish

Not sure I understand the bug report.  It seems to be doing exactly what it is supposed to - the user asked to "tolerate" unready endpoints, so it is.  "tolerate" is maybe not the best word here, but still..

@thockin @bgrant0607's primary concern is that we're misusing the API. We're adding an unready address to the ready Addresses of the EndpointSubsets to create a SRV record so that stateful Pods can find their peers in a StatefulSet. The API already lets us register the unready endpoints for the headless service in the EndpointSubset's NotReadyAddresses. We should be detecting the annotation/field in kube-dns and adding NotReadyAddresses there. The users desire should be realized by the DNS implementation. More context [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/49061).

The current annotation explicitly says "tell everyone these endpoints are
ready" (which has a specific meaning, i.e. put me in rotation), so that
clients don't have to know the difference.  It forces legacy clients to
behave correctly.  Making a client respect the bool and interpret unready
endpoints would not transparently work for legacy clients.

I think the latter behavior is more correct, but the only difference
between the two approaches is whether the author can force legacy clients
to do what they expect, vs hope and wait for clients to be updated.

wrote:

> EndpointSubsets to create a SRV record so that stateful Pods can find their
> peers in a StatefulSet. The API already lets us register the unready
> endpoints for the headless service in the EndpointSubset's
> NotReadyAddresses. We should be detecting the annotation/field in kube-dns
> and adding NotReadyAddresses there. The users desire should be realized by

> .
>

@smarterclayton I think the correctness of the behavior with respect to the use of Addresses vs UnreadyAddresses is @bgrant0607's primary concern.

@thockin @smarterclayton @bgrant0607 @erictune I would like to propose the following.

1. As a first step, we keep the current behavior of the endpoints controller and promote the annotation to a TolerateUnreadyEndpoints field.
    1. This will be a breaking API change with respect to the alpha annotation, but it will not modify the current behavior of the endpoint controller or require modification of any DNS addons.
    1. If we don't promote the field to at least beta, we can't reasonably expect that any DNS addons should modify their behavior to use it.
1. We (the community) modify all DNS addons to use the TolerateUnreadyEndpoints field to decide if they will add EndpointSubsets in the UnreadyAddresses to HeadlessServices.
    1. As the endpoint controller has not yet been modified this code will go into production dark.
    1. It would, by design, be compatible with current endpoint controller implementation and the modification proposed below.
1. We modify the endpoint controller to ignore the TolerateUnreadyEndpoints field, and pass the responsibility of implementing the TolerateUnreadyEndpoints behavior to the DNS addons.
    1. This will be a breaking, behavioral change, so we'd have to give DNS addon implementers time to adapt.

Alternatively we could
1. Leave the annotation as an alpha annotation.
1. Require that all DNS providers always add the UnreadyAddresses of EndpointSubsets for Headless Services.
    1. We're just adding a SRV here so this will be safe provided that clients of the HeadlessService don't require that only ready Pods should be added to DNS.
1. When all of the DNS addons have been updated, remove the alpha annotation and modify the endpoint controller.

I prefer the first approach because:
1. It was previously decided to promote the annotation, and it was indicated to the community that this is what we would deliver.
1. It gives us time to update the DNS addons, while allowing us to promote the functionality in such a way that users can depend on its consistent behavior.
1. If we never do steps 2 and 3, we have a working solution that can be advanced to GA.
1. If we do have a StatefulSet that requires readiness as a precondition for being added to DNS we support it.

The approach does have drawbacks:
1. We have to live with the TolerateUnreadyEndpoints field for the lifetime of v1.Service.
1. The second approach is simpler provided we are willing to live with the idea that StatefulSet Pods have to be able to determine the readiness of their peers without the help of a DNS addon that respects readiness checks (this is true for the majority of what is available today).

While the second approach benefits from simplicity it  also has downsides:
1. As previously mentioned, if we add DNS entries for UnreadyAddresses the Pods of StatefulSets must not depend on readiness to be communicated via DNS. 
1. We've left the annotation in alpha so long that it has been cargo culted into every StatefulSet example, into the stable helm repo, and into production (granted StatefulSet is still beta). I don't see how continuing to leave this annotation as alpha will help us.
1. Its an all or nothing, break both the existing alpha annotation and current behavior concurrently change.  This does not break our guarantees given that the annotation (and therefore the behavior) can be considered to be alpha, but it's highly probable that we'd be shipping v1.StatefulSet with dependencies on an alpha annotation we intend to deprecate.

@bgrant0607 That approach SGTM, we would have to
1. Ship the annotation in 1.8
1. Move all the consumers (DNS addons, helm charts, examples etc) to use the field 1.9 and deprecate the annotation.
1. Remove the annotation in 1.10.

The only downside is that we will continue to carry the annotation for another 2 releases, and the cargo cult is likely to grow.
We should also announce that the annotation is deprecated in 1.8.

I don't think this feature is just about DNS.  There are other clients of Endpoints, and this behavior catches them all.  I ACK that it's a little unintuitive, but frankly, "UnreadyEndpoints" is weird too.  I'd rather we never added that, and we just added a bool or annotation indicating whether readiness is considered important or not.

TL;DR - I think the current behavior is as correct as this is going to get.
Many discovery APIs (e.g., Consul's, Eureka) include readiness/health information as a first-class property. It would be a shame to lose that.

Two different consumers of a service can care about different sets of
endpoints (I don't remember if that had been brought back up on this
thread).  Forcing me to create multiple sets of services is a bit tedious.

@kow3ns is this still an issue? I believe it is.
/remove-lifecycle rotten
We need to take this into account when we redesign the Endpoints API
@freehan Can you digest this issue, make sure new Endpoints work addresses it (or explicitly does not) and then close?
@freehan - are we happy with new API wrt this?

I am leaning towards the 1st proposal in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/49239#issuecomment-319501404

That means the new EndpointSlice controller will just ignore the `tolerate-unready-endpoint` annotation. Essentially, this decouples the DNS and endpoints. 

However, I am not sure if there is use case for `tolerate-unready-endpoint` on the service endpoint side.

I don't see how that proposal works for non-DNS related consumers of these addresses. For example, won't unready addresses be programmed for cluster IP services when the field/annotation is used? This means kube-proxy or any other consumer will now have to re-implement the "tolerate unready" logic.

It looks like the new `PublishNotReadyAddresses` field is explicitly for DNS. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.16.0-alpha.3/pkg/apis/core/types.go#L3432

Please correct me if I am wrong, the proposal is NOT to support "tolerate unready" on the kube-proxy side. Unless there is real use cases.

It already is supported in kube-proxy. It's done by the endpoints controller. By the time it gets to kube-proxy, the decision is already made and so kube-proxy doesn't do anything special (neither does CoreDNS for that matter):

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/endpoint/endpoints_controller.go#L614
That said, it doesn't mean we *have* to support it the same way in endpoint slice - it's a different API after all. But we need consciously decide to not support it, if that's the case.

The stateful set use case is one, but I at least also used this feature at one point for pods that had a control port and a data port (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/49239#issuecomment-351087689).

I wonder if the implicit "a pod is ready means the endpoint is ready" is just not the right model. Something more akin to the pod readiness gates but for service endpoints would be more flexible. So, "endpoint is ready if it meets these conditions" - where "pod readiness" is one possible condition, but other pod conditions could be looked at as well.

That's obviously a more complicated solution, but would allow folks to define "readiness" for their endpoints however they need for their particular use case (with the default being the current endpoint readiness == pod readiness).

Maybe a follow-on feature, if needed.

Yes. Agreed. 

I was thinking extending Pod ReadinessGate to allow user to specify if a pod readiness gate can block endpoint readiness or not. That would allow user to achieve something like "endpoint is ready" but "pod is not ready" when "all containers are ready" but "pod readiness gate is not ready but not blocking endpoint readiness". 

I feel like the readiness life cycle has to anchor on pods for backward compatibility because workflows only consider pods and none considers endpoint readiness.

This would be a separate feature any way.

title: Kube-proxy facing locking timeout in large clusters during load test with services enabled
body:
Follows from discussion in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/48052

We noticed this while performing load test on 4000 node clusters with services enabled. The iptables restore step in the proxier fails with:
```
E0625 09:03:14.873338       5 proxier.go:1574] Failed to execute iptables-restore: failed to acquire old iptables lock: timed out waiting for the condition
```

And the reason quite likely is because of "huge" size of iptables (tens of MBs) as we run 30 pods per node and each pod is part of exactly one service
=> 30 * 4000 = 120k service endpoints (and these updates happen on all 4000 nodes)

cc @kubernetes/sig-network-misc @kubernetes/sig-scalability-misc @danwinship @wojtek-t

nodes.body: fyi, the logs for the run are here - http://gcsweb.k8s.io/gcs/kubernetes-jenkins/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-enormous-cluster/10/

I suspect other components are holding the lock and fail to release. 
Is kube-proxy able to have successful iptables-restore after first occurence?
@freehan It's failing continuously (https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-jenkins/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-enormous-cluster/10/artifacts/e2e-enormous-cluster-minion-group-01nl/kube-proxy.log)
Linking issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/47344 for tracking.
cc @wojtek-t
Are the nodes running on CVM or COS? It looks like it is running on CVM, right?
Is there anyway we can execute `lsof` on a node in the bad state?
It looks like iptables util cannot open a specific linux domain socket. I suspect kube-proxy failed to close it during one run. Not sure why. I will send a PR to expose the error soon.
@freehan The nodes were running on gci (which I guess is the same as cos). Ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/jobs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-enormous-cluster.env#L33

May be related https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/45385.

I tried to find the dashboard where the enormous node test + services-enabled is. Can anyone provide a pointer to the testgrid runs?

The job for gce 5k-node performance test - https://k8s-testgrid.appspot.com/google-gce-scale#gce-scale-performance
It's not automated yet, but I'm manually triggering the job almost everyday (fixing some bugs each time) until the test goes green.
And regarding services, we reduced it to half of the original no. (which was 16400) without changing total no. of pods involved in services (ref https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/48908), just to experiment.

So I just remembered this issue today and re-looked into our 5k-node scalability tests (where we're creating 150k backends). The problem with iptables-restore is still seen. <kube-proxy starts around 08:14>
```
...
I0615 08:37:51.983992       1 service.go:309] Adding new service port "e2e-tests-load-30-nodepods-2-b4xz2/load-small-1-svc:" at 10.0.79.86:80/TCP

keeps adding more services ports...
and after a while starts seeing...
E0615 10:21:27.950023       1 proxier.go:1306] Failed to execute iptables-restore: failed to acquire old iptables lock: timed out waiting for the condition

```

I looked into couple other kube-proxies and all of them start seeing these errors at similar time (~10:30). So my feeling is that the kube-proxies are tripping after iptables reaches a "critical mass". This is bad as it might be that some endpoints never get programmed after a limit.

I'll try experimenting with half the no. of endpoints and see.
/assign

> I see this error message fairly often with low hundreds of services, not 120k

@joeldeaguero To clarify - 120k I mentioned above is not no. of services, it's no. of backends (or endpoints).

There were kernel problems with large iptables tables at some point... I don't know when the slowness was first introduced, other than that a year ago or so the current mainline kernel exhibited the problem but the current Ubuntu LTS kernel didn't. It's fixed in 4.15.

@shyamjvs - about your comment with logs - I looked into the code and those errors are basically coming from these file:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/util/iptables/iptables_linux.go#L84

In particular, that means that we have an artificial 2s timeout here, which may or may not be justified at scale. We need to check what exactly it does and why it fails?

Maybe the problem is that some previous calls to iptables restore/save were interrupted and didn't return the lock?

BTW - looking into those logs, I think it's not the case that we stopped being able to acquire the lock - it's just that *some* attempts to acquire it were failing. Otherwise this would have happen much more frequently.

May be worth adding a log here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/util/iptables/iptables_linux.go#L87
to see why we're failing to acquire that lock.
I'll take a look later today/tomorrow when I find time. Thanks for those leads.

I looked a bit into that, and my personal guess is that during that times Kubelet is actually altering with iptables (hostport manager in Kubelet).

If my hypothesis is correct, problem the easiest way to fix that is to bump this timeout (I guess with that big iptables, iptables-restore may take more than 2s).

One useful thing to do might be to start tracking how long iptables updating takes (i.e. if iptables-restore takes more than X seconds, log a long run) - let me send out a PR for that.

title: Api docs wrong for service name
body:


I think we'll have to clone ObjectMeta and other shared types eventually, but we could add a note to the share documentation about service names.

I'd love to make time (or for someone else to make time) to make the
go->swagger process do the right thing for cases like:

```
type Foo struct {
    OM struct {
        // Usual comment here
        ObjectMeta `json:",inline"`
        // Different Comment Here
        Name string
    } `json:"metadata"`
```

and to see us do more of this sort of inlining, rather than type-sharing.
I think it makes docs clearer too.
